LYMPHOID / IMMUNE__Thymus:
Overview — School for T Cells

The thymus is a primary lymphoid organ where T lymphocytes mature and are selected. It is large in childhood and involutes (replaced by fat) after puberty.

🔬 Image slot — thymus with cortex (dense), medulla (pale) and a Hassall's corpuscle
  • Divided into lobules with a dark cortex (densely packed immature T cells/thymocytes) and pale medulla
  • Epithelial reticular cells form the framework and the blood–thymus barrier (cortex)
  • Hassall's corpuscles = whorls of keratinised epithelial reticular cells in the medulla (the diagnostic feature)
  • Positive & negative selection removes useless/self-reactive T cells
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
DiGeorge syndrome
Thymic aplasia (22q11 deletion) → absent T cells → immunodeficiency.
Thymoma
Epithelial tumour; associated with myasthenia gravis.
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • Thymus = primary lymphoid organ; T-cell maturation & selection; involutes after puberty.
  • Hassall's corpuscles = medulla (the give-away); cortex is densely packed with thymocytes.
  • DiGeorge = thymic aplasia (no T cells); thymoma → myasthenia gravis.
LYMPHOID / IMMUNE__Lymph Node:
Overview — The Lymph Filter

Lymph nodes filter lymph and mount adaptive immune responses. Lymph flows in through afferent vessels, percolates through the node, and leaves via a single efferent vessel at the hilum.

🔬 Image slot — lymph node: cortex with germinal-centre follicles, paracortex, medulla
RegionContains
CortexB-cell follicles; active ones have pale germinal centres
ParacortexT cells + high endothelial venules (lymphocyte entry) + dendritic cells
MedullaMedullary cords (plasma cells) + sinuses (macrophages)
Reactive Changes
Follicular hyperplasia (big germinal centres) → B-cell/antibody response
Paracortical hyperplasia → T-cell (e.g. viral) response
Sinus histiocytosis → draining nearby inflammation/tumour
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Lymphoma
Effaced architecture; Hodgkin (Reed–Sternberg cells) vs non-Hodgkin.
Metastasis
Carcinoma spreads to regional nodes (subcapsular sinus first).
Granulomatous nodes
TB (caseating) / sarcoidosis (non-caseating).
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • Cortex = B-cell follicles (germinal centres); paracortex = T cells (+ HEVs); medulla = plasma cells + macrophages.
  • Lymph: afferent (many) → sinuses → efferent (one) at the hilum.
  • Follicular hyperplasia = B response; paracortical = T (viral); Reed–Sternberg = Hodgkin lymphoma.
LYMPHOID / IMMUNE__Spleen:
Overview — Red Pulp + White Pulp

The spleen filters blood (unlike nodes, which filter lymph): it removes old red cells and mounts immune responses. Two compartments: red pulp and white pulp.

🔬 Image slot — spleen: white-pulp nodules (with central arterioles) among red pulp
Red pulp
  • Splenic (venous) sinusoids + cords of Billroth packed with red cells & macrophages
  • Filters/removes old or abnormal red cells; recycles iron
White pulp
  • Lymphoid tissue around central arterioles: PALS (T cells) + lymphoid follicles (B cells)
  • Immune surveillance of blood
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Hyposplenism / splenectomy
Risk of overwhelming sepsis by encapsulated organisms; Howell–Jolly bodies on film.
Splenomegaly
Portal hypertension, haemolysis, infection, infiltration.
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • Spleen filters blood: red pulp (cords of Billroth + sinusoids; removes old RBCs) + white pulp (PALS = T cells, follicles = B cells around central arterioles).
  • Post-splenectomy → encapsulated-organism sepsis (vaccinate!) & Howell–Jolly bodies.
LYMPHOID / IMMUNE__Tonsils:
Overview

Tonsils are aggregates of lymphoid tissue guarding the entrance to the pharynx (part of MALT). They are partially encapsulated and have no afferent lymphatics.

🔬 Image slot — palatine tonsil: stratified squamous epithelium dipping into crypts over lymphoid follicles
  • Palatine tonsils: covered by stratified squamous epithelium that dips into deep crypts, overlying lymphoid follicles with germinal centres
  • Sample antigens from inhaled/ingested material
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Tonsillitis
Infection → enlarged, inflamed tonsils; recurrent disease may need tonsillectomy.
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • Palatine tonsil = stratified squamous epithelium + crypts over lymphoid follicles (part of MALT).
  • Partially encapsulated; no afferent lymphatics (samples antigen directly from the surface).
LYMPHOID / IMMUNE__Mucosa-Associated Lym:
Overview

MALT is unencapsulated lymphoid tissue guarding mucosal surfaces (gut, airway, urogenital tract) — the immune system's front line at body surfaces.

🔬 Image slot — Peyer's patch in the ileum with a dome and M cells
  • Examples: Peyer's patches (ileum), tonsils, appendix, bronchus-associated (BALT)
  • Specialised M (microfold) cells in the overlying epithelium sample luminal antigen and pass it to underlying lymphoid follicles
  • Produces secretory IgA, the main mucosal antibody
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
MALT lymphoma
Gastric MALT lymphoma driven by H. pylori — may regress on eradication.
Portal of entry
M cells are exploited by some pathogens (e.g. Salmonella) to invade.
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • MALT = unencapsulated mucosal lymphoid tissue (Peyer's patches, tonsils, appendix, BALT).
  • M cells sample luminal antigen; MALT produces secretory IgA.
  • Gastric MALT lymphoma → H. pylori (may regress with eradication).
LYMPHOID / IMMUNE__Bone Marrow (red & ye:
Overview

Bone marrow fills the medullary cavities and is the site of haematopoiesis and B-cell maturation. It comes in two forms: red (active) and yellow (fatty).

🔬 Image slot — bone marrow trephine: haematopoietic cells, fat spaces and a megakaryocyte
Red marrow
  • Haematopoietically active; cords of developing blood cells + megakaryocytes between sinusoids
  • In adults: axial skeleton, pelvis, proximal femur/humerus
Yellow marrow
  • Fatty, inactive; can reconvert to red marrow when demand rises
Marrow is a primary lymphoid organ too — the site where B cells (and all blood cells) are made.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Leukaemia
Marrow packed with blasts → failure of normal haematopoiesis (anaemia, infection, bleeding).
Aplastic anaemia
Hypocellular (fatty) marrow → pancytopenia.
Myelofibrosis / infiltration
Fibrous or tumour replacement → extramedullary haematopoiesis.
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • Marrow = site of haematopoiesis + B-cell maturation (a primary lymphoid organ).
  • Red = active; yellow = fatty/inactive (reconverts on demand); adult red marrow = axial skeleton.
  • Megakaryocytes are the large cells that shed platelets.
  • Leukaemia = marrow packed with blasts; aplastic anaemia = fatty hypocellular marrow.
